summary: Describes the tunnel broker model, which helps early IPv6 adopters connect to an existing IPv6 network such as the 6bone and obtain stable IPv6 addresses and DNS names. A broker sets up the tunnel on the user's behalf. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The IPv6 Tunnel Broker is a service for people who have IPv4 but want IPv6. A broker on the Internet sets up the tunnel for them, hands out an IPv6 address and a DNS name, and keeps the tunnel running. RFC 3053 describes how such a service could be built.

subtitle: A service that sets up IPv6 tunnels for people who only have IPv4

tldr.problem: IPv6 networks of the time were built on tunnels carried over IPv4, and configuring those tunnels by hand was too much work for an isolated end user who simply had an IPv4 connection and wanted to join the IPv6 world.
tldr.mechanism: A tunnel broker acts as a service. The user registers, gives its IPv4 address and a DNS name, and the broker picks a tunnel server, allocates an IPv6 prefix, registers the addresses in the DNS, configures the far end of the tunnel and hands the settings back to the user.
tldr.outcome: The user gets a stable IPv6 address and DNS name even from a dial-up connection with a changing IPv4 address. The memo defines a framework rather than a protocol, and says plainly that the model does not work behind a NAT box using private IPv4 addresses.

today: RFC 3053 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a framework rather than a protocol, written while the 6bone was the main experimental IPv6 network, so it reads as a record of one approach to the IPv6 transition.

sections.title: Why a Tunnel Broker
sections.content:
The IPv6 Internet of the time was built largely on tunnels carried over the existing IPv4 network. Those tunnels are difficult to configure and maintain at scale, because an administrator has to do extensive manual configuration for each one.

Large sites and Internet service providers had shown they could manage that, but the memo argues the process is too complex for an isolated end user who already has an IPv4 connection and would like to join the IPv6 world. The tunnel broker model is meant to help early IPv6 adopters connect to an existing IPv6 network such as the 6bone and get stable, permanent IPv6 addresses and DNS names.

Other transition mechanisms already existed. Automatic tunnels with IPv4-compatible addresses give simple early connectivity between isolated dual-stack hosts and routers, but they do not solve IPv4 address exhaustion, and there is a fear of pulling the complete IPv4 routing table into the IPv6 world, which would multiply the routing table size problem by five. 6over4 is a site-local mechanism that uses IPv4 multicast as a virtual link layer; it does not connect an isolated user to the global IPv6 Internet. 6to4 lets isolated IPv6 domains reach each other with minimal manual configuration by embedding IPv4 tunnel addresses into IPv6 prefixes.

The broker serves a different part of the IPv6 community. It fits small isolated sites, and especially isolated hosts on the IPv4 Internet, that want to reach an existing IPv6 network. The 6to4 approach instead suits isolated sites that want to reach each other without waiting for their IPv4 providers to deliver native IPv6, which suits extranets and virtual private networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Early IPv6 networks were built by tunnelling IPv6 traffic inside IPv4 packets. Setting those tunnels up was hard work, and it was too much to ask of a single home user who just wanted to try IPv6. A tunnel broker is a service that does the work on the user's behalf and hands out an IPv6 address and a name for it.

sections.title: The Tunnel Broker Model
sections.content:
The model has three functional elements plus the user. A tunnel broker (TB) is where the user registers and activates tunnels; it manages tunnel creation, modification and deletion on the user's behalf and may also register the user's IPv6 address and name in the DNS. A tunnel server (TS) is a dual-stack router connected to the global Internet; on a configuration order from the broker it creates, modifies or deletes the server side of each tunnel, and it may maintain usage statistics for every active tunnel. The DNS holds the global addresses and names of the tunnels. The user is a dual-stack host or router already connected to the IPv4 Internet.

For scalability the broker can share the network-side tunnel endpoints among several tunnel servers, sending configuration orders to whichever server is relevant. The broker must be addressable over IPv4; it may also be addressable over IPv6, but that is not mandatory, and the connections between broker and servers can use either.

The broker can be seen as a virtual IPv6 provider. In that role it lets an IPv6 provider apply its own access policies to the network resources its users consume.
sections.plainLanguage: The service has three parts. The broker is the desk where users sign up and where their tunnels are created and removed. The tunnel server is the machine at the far end of the tunnel, a router that speaks both IPv4 and IPv6. The DNS holds the addresses and names. The user is a computer that already has IPv4 and learns to speak IPv6 through the tunnel.

sections.title: Signing Up and Getting a Tunnel
sections.content:
The client is a dual-stack node connected to the IPv4 Internet. Before anything else it must give the broker its identity and credentials, so that the broker can authenticate and authorize the user and optionally do accounting, for example using existing AAA facilities such as RADIUS. The client and the broker need a pre-configured or automatically established security association, so that nobody else can use the service.

Once authorized, the client provides at least three things: the IPv4 address of its side of the tunnel, a name to register in the DNS for the global IPv6 address assigned to that end, and whether it is a standalone host or a router. A client that is an IPv6 router serving several IPv6 hosts also says how many addresses it needs, so the broker can allocate a prefix that fits instead of a single address.

The broker then does a fixed list of things. It designates a tunnel server to act as the network-side endpoint, choosing it by some load-sharing rule set by the broker administrator. It chooses the IPv6 prefix to allocate, whose length can be anything between 0 and 128, with 48 for a site prefix, 64 for a subnet prefix and 128 for a host prefix the most common. It fixes a lifetime for the tunnel. It registers the assigned global IPv6 addresses in the DNS. It configures the server side of the tunnel. And it notifies the client of the configuration information, including the tunnel parameters and the DNS names. When the client side has also been configured, the tunnel is up and the user can reach the 6bone or any other IPv6 network the tunnel server is connected to.
sections.plainLanguage: To start, the user proves who they are and gives the broker three things: the IPv4 address of their end of the tunnel, a name for their new IPv6 address, and whether their machine is a computer or a router. The broker then picks a server, allocates an address, sets an expiry time, records the address in the DNS, sets up the far end of the tunnel and tells the user what to configure.

sections.title: Addresses, Lifetimes and Limits
sections.content:
Both ends of every tunnel get global IPv6 addresses from the address space the broker manages. Their lifetime should be relatively long, and potentially longer than the lifetime of the user's IPv4 connection, so that a user on a dial-up link with a dynamically assigned IPv4 address still holds a semipermanent IPv6 address and DNS name.

Active tunnels consume memory and processing time on the tunnel servers, so unused tunnels should be kept to a minimum. Each tunnel should have a lifetime and be removed when it expires, unless the client asks for an extension. The memo notes that this is not ideal for short-lived dial-up connections, where a new tunnel is likely to be used briefly and then never again, because every time the user reconnects they get a new IPv4 address and must either set up a new tunnel or update the previous one.

Two remedies are offered. The tunnel server can report traffic and reachability statistics for every active tunnel to the broker, which can then delete a tunnel after a period of inactivity without waiting for the longer lifetime to run out. Or a keep-alive mechanism between the client and the server or broker can release a tunnel as soon as the user disconnects, at the cost of a software upgrade on the client. Keeping the configuration after a disconnect has its own value: when the user reconnects, possibly from a different IPv4 address, the broker can order the server to re-create the tunnel with the new address and reuse the previously allocated IPv6 addresses, so the user keeps a nearly permanent IPv6 address and its DNS name.

One limitation is stated plainly. The mechanism may not work if the user is using private IPv4 addresses behind a NAT box.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv6 addresses are meant to last longer than the user's IPv4 connection, so a dial-up user keeps the same address and name even when the provider gives them a new IPv4 address each time they connect. Because idle tunnels waste server resources, the broker should expire them, either on a timer or when the server reports that a tunnel has stopped carrying traffic.

sections.title: How the Pieces Could Talk to Each Other
sections.content:
The memo does not specify protocols for the interactions between the entities, but it lists workable options. Between the user and the broker, HTTP could carry the exchange, with the user filling in forms on a web server and the server replying with an HTML page stating that the server end-point is configured and showing the tunnel information. The simplest way to configure the client is for the broker to prepare personalised activation and de-activation scripts to run offline on the client machine; that needs no client software, but it raises security concerns because a user may find it hard to verify that a downloaded script does nothing illegal or dangerous once it runs.

To avoid that, the memo suggests defining a new MIME content type, for example application/tunnel, so the tunnel parameters are delivered as data rather than as a script, with a dedicated agent on the client to set the tunnel endpoint up. Between the broker and the tunnel servers, the options include a set of simple RSH commands over IPsec, SNMP, or any other network management solution. Between the broker and the DNS, the memo recommends the Dynamic DNS Update protocol, used to add or delete AAAA, A6 and PTR records in the zone reserved for broker users, with a simpler alternative of RSH commands against the authoritative name server.

One open issue remains: real use of the service may require accounting and billing functions.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not fix the protocols, but it suggests practical choices. The user talks to the broker over the web. The broker talks to the tunnel servers with a network management protocol or simple commands over an encrypted link. The broker updates the DNS with the standard dynamic update protocol. For the client, sending a small data file with the settings is safer than sending a script to run.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All three interactions have to be secured: user to broker, broker to tunnel server, and broker to DNS. The technique depends on the implementation. For the user-to-broker link, HTTP allows widely adopted features such as SSL to encrypt the data sent to and downloaded from the web server, and makes it possible to rely on simple username and password authentication and on existing AAA facilities such as RADIUS for access control. For the broker-to-server link, secure SNMP could be adopted. If dynamic DNS update is used for the broker-to-DNS link, the security issues are the ones described for Secure Domain Name System Dynamic Update; otherwise standard IPsec mechanisms can be applied to the RSH approach.

Two further points are raised. If the client configuration is done by running scripts provided by the broker, those scripts must run with enough privilege to manage network interfaces, such as an administrator or root role, which is dangerous and should be considered only for early implementations; transferring the tunnel configuration parameters in a MIME type over HTTPS is a more secure approach. And a loss of confidentiality can occur whenever a dial-up user disconnects without tearing down the tunnel, because the tunnel server keeps forwarding IPv6 traffic to the user's old IPv4 address, which may since have been assigned to another subscriber of the same dial-up provider; the keep-alive mechanism would let the broker stop forwarding at once.

Finally, the broker must protect itself against denial of service attacks, in which a malicious user asks for many tunnels at once and exhausts the resources of the tunnel server. Administratively limiting the number of tunnels that a single user may set up at the same time is one possible protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Every conversation in the service has to be protected, and the memo lists the tools for each one: encrypted web pages and RADIUS for the user, secure SNMP or IPsec for the tunnel servers, and secure dynamic updates for the name server. It also warns against running downloaded scripts with administrator rights, notes that a stale tunnel can send traffic to the wrong dial-up customer, and asks the broker to cap how many tunnels one user may open.
